1.note: Isaiah is using the word translated as **it happened** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event. Alternate translation: [Now in the days of Ahaz]
The word **Ahaz** is the name of a man. He was king of Judah.

Here the author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture. See how the UST models this.
The word **Jotham** is the name of a man. He was the father of **Ahaz** and had been a **king of Judah**.
The word **Uzziah** is the name of a man. He was the father of **Jotham** and had been a **king of Judah**.
The word **Rezin** is the name of a man. He was the king of Aram.
The word **Pekah** is the name of a man. He was the **king of Israel**.
The word **Remaliah** is the name of a man. He was the father of **Pekah**.
The pronoun **he** refers to **Rezin**. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Rezin was not able to battle against Jerusalem]

Isaiah uses the word **but** here to indicate a contrast between Rezin and Pekah going up to battle against Jerusalem and their inability to conquer it. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. See how the UST models this.

2.note: The expression **it was declared** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And news reached the house of David]

Isaiah is speaking of the royal dynasty of **David** as if it were a **house**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the royal family of David]

The names **Aram** and **Ephraim** represent the armies of those nations. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the armies of Aram have settled upon Ephraim]

Isaiah is speaking of the emotions of Ahaz and his people as if the **heart** were a physical object that could shake. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And Ahaz trembled with fear, and his people trembled]
The pronoun **his** refers to Ahaz. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And Ahaz’s heart shook]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the trees of the forest** shake uncontrollably when the **wind** blows, so Ahaz and his people were trembling with fear. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [just as the trees of a forest shake uncontrollably when the wind blows against them]

3.note: The word **Shear-Jashub** is the name of a boy. It means “a remnant will return.” Isaiah echoes the meaning of this name in 10:21 when he says, “A remnant will return.” To help your readers appreciate this, you may wish to explain the meaning of this name in a footnote.

A conduit is a kind of channel built to carry water. If your readers would not be familiar with what a conduit is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [the aqueduct]

4.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [that he should guard himself and be quiet]

The words translated as **Guard yourself and be quiet** are imperatives, but they communicate encouragement rather than commands. If the imperatives do not communicate encouragement for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates encouragement. Alternate translation: [May you guard yourself and be quiet]

The expression translated as **May you not fear** is an imperative, but it communicates encouragement rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate encouragement for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates encouragement. Alternate translation: [Fear not]

Yahweh is speaking of Ahaz’s possible loss of courage as if his heart could physically soften. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and may you not lose your courage]

Yahweh is speaking of **Rezin** and Pekah as if they were smoking stubs of firewood that are almost burned out and no longer dangerous. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [nearly burnt-out and harmless men]

Yahweh is using **the burning of the nose** as a common expression of the culture to mean “anger.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [by the anger of]

5.q: יָעַ֥ץ עָלֶ֛י⁠ךָ אֲרָ֖ם רָעָ֑ה אֶפְרַ֥יִם וּ⁠בֶן־רְמַלְיָ֖הוּ
5.note: The names **Aram** and **Ephraim** represent the leaders of those nations. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the king of Aram has plotted harm against you, along with the son of Remaliah, king of Israel]

6.note: The king of Aram is saying what he wants the Israelite king to do. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [I desire that we go up against Judah] or [We should go up against Judah]

The name **Judah** represents the people of that nation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Let us go up against the nation of Judah]
The word **Tabeel** is the name of the father of the man they want to be king of Judah.

7.note: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of clauses in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [It will not stand, no, it will not be] or [This well never happen!]

8.note: Here, **the head** represents the capital city. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Damascus is the capital city of Aram]

Here, **the head** represents the chief ruler. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and the ruler of Damascus is Rezin]
Translate this number according to the conventions of your own language and culture. Alternate translation: [sixty-five years]

The expression **will be shattered** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [enemies will shatter Ephraim so that it is no longer a people]

9.note: Here, **the head** represents the capital city. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And the capital of Ephraim is Samaria … and the ruler of Samaria is the son of Remaliah]

Here, **the head** represents the chief ruler. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the chief ruler of Samaria {is} the son of Remaliah]

The words translated as **believe** and **established** sound very similar in Hebrew. It is often difficult to reproduce this kind of word play in another language, but if your language does have similar terms that you can use in these instances, it would be appropriate to do that in your translation. If not, you could show the emphasis in another way. For example, some versions say “surely” instead of “then” to reflect how the wordplay makes this a stronger statement. Alternate translation: [If you do not believe, surely you will not be established]

The expression **you will not be established** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [God will not establish you]

This is the end of a multi-level quotation structure. You may wish to mark the ending of each speech level with closing quotation marks or with some other punctuation or convention that your language uses. This is modeled in both the ULT and the UST.

11.note: The word translated as **Ask** is an imperative, but it communicates an invitation rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate an invitation for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates an invitation. Alternate translation: [Please ask Yahweh your God for a sign] or [You may ask a sign for yourself from Yahweh your God]

Yahweh is referring to the entire range of possible signs by naming two extremes, **Make deep to Sheol** and **make high to above**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Anywhere from the depths of Sheol to the heights of the sky]

12.note: Ahaz actually means to communicate the opposite of the literal meaning of what he is saying here. He appears to be honoring Yahweh by not testing him, but he is actually refusing to obey Yahweh’s command. If a speaker of your language would not do that, you could translate the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I refuse to ask, and I refuse to test Yahweh]

13.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 7:2.

Isaiah is speaking of God as if he were a person who could become weary. He means that Ahaz’s disobedience tests God’s patience. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you test my God’s patience]

13.q: הַ⁠מְעַ֤ט מִ⁠כֶּם֙ הַלְא֣וֹת אֲנָשִׁ֔ים כִּ֥י תַלְא֖וּ גַּ֥ם אֶת־אֱלֹהָֽ⁠י
13.note: Isaiah is using the question form to rebuke Ahaz. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You make man weary, and you also make my God weary!]

14.note: The pronoun **you** here is plural and refers to the house of David, not just to Ahaz alone. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the Lord himself will give a sign to you all]

Yahweh is using the term **Behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Pay attention]

The word **Immanuel** is the name of a boy. It means “God with us.” Isaiah echoes this name in 8:10 when he says “God is with us.” To help your readers appreciate this, you may wish to explain the meaning of this name in a footnote.

15.note: The term **curds** describes solids that form out of milk. If your readers would not be familiar with what curds are, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [milk solids]

Isaiah is using the adjectives **evil** and **good** as nouns to mean certain kinds of things. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [to refuse what is evil and to choose what is good]

16.note: The expression **the land will be forsaken** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [people will abandon the land]

Isaiah is using from the faces of as a common expression of the culture to mean “because of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [because of the two kings of it]

The pronoun **you** refers to Ahaz, and the pronoun **it** refers to the land of the two kings. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [you, Ahaz, dread because of the two kings of that land]

17.note: Isaiah is speaking of the family and descendants of Ahaz’s father as if they were a **house.** Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the family of your father]

17.q: יָבִ֨יא יְהוָ֜ה עָלֶ֗י⁠ךָ וְ⁠עַֽל־עַמְּ⁠ךָ֮ וְ⁠עַל־בֵּ֣ית אָבִי⁠ךָ֒ יָמִים֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר לֹא־בָ֔אוּ לְ⁠מִ⁠יּ֥וֹם סוּר־אֶפְרַ֖יִם מֵ⁠עַ֣ל יְהוּדָ֑ה אֵ֖ת מֶ֥לֶךְ אַשּֽׁוּר
17.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about **the king of Assyria** before the information about **the days** that **Yahweh will bring**. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will use the king of Assyria to bring upon you and upon your people and upon the house of your father days that have not come since the day of the turning of Ephraim away from Judah]

18.note: Isaiah is using the word translated as **it will happen** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.
To translate the phrase **in that day** here and in the rest of this chapter, see how you translated it in [4:1](ta:04).

Isaiah is speaking of the armies of **Egypt** and **Assyria** as if they were a fly and a bee that Yahweh could summon by whistling. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will call for the army of Egypt … and for the army of Assyria]

19.note: Isaiah is speaking of the invading armies as if they were insects that settle down in every crevice of the land. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly.
The pronoun **they** refers to the armies of Egypt and Assyria, which are described in the previous verse as “the fly” and “the bee.” It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers.
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of desolation, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [desolate land]

Isaiah says **in all of the thornbushes and in all of the watering holes** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [and everywhere you look]

20.q: יְגַלַּ֣ח אֲדֹנָ⁠י֩ בְּ⁠תַ֨עַר הַ⁠שְּׂכִירָ֜ה בְּ⁠עֶבְרֵ֤י נָהָר֙
20.note: Isaiah is speaking of the Lord’s judgment on Judah as if he would **shave** it **with a razor**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the Lord will strip the land bare with a razor hired from beyond the Euphrates River]

The expression **hired from beyond the River** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [with a razor that someone has hired from beyond the River]

Isaiah is referring to the whole body by naming two extremes, **the head and the hair of the feet**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the hair of the entire body]

Isaiah is using the phrase **the hair of the feet** as a polite way of referring to the private parts of the body. If it would be helpful for your readers, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the hair of the private parts]
The pronoun **it** refers to the **razor**. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the razor will also take away the beard]

21.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 7:2.

Isaiah is not referring to a specific man. He means any person in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [a person will keep alive a calf]

22.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of abundance, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the overflow]

Isaiah is not referring to a specific person by the pronoun **he**. Here, Isaiah means any person left in the land. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [anyone will eat curds]

23.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 7:18.
Translate this number according to the conventions of your own language and culture. Alternate translation: [a thousand vines valued at a thousand silver coins]

The terms **briar** and **thorn** mean similar things. Isaiah is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [thorny weeds]

24.note: The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [because]

Isaiah is not referring to a specific **One**. He means anyone in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [People will come there with arrows and with a bow]
See how you translated the similar expression in 7:23.

25.note: The expression **were hoed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And all of the hills that farmers hoed with a hoe]

Here, the first use of **for** marks **the sending out of the ox** and the second use of **for** marks **the trampling of the sheep** as the purpose that the land will serve. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. See the UST.
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of fear, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because you dread the]
See how you translated the similar expression in 7:23.
